nameStory: The African Collared-Dove gets its name from its native homeland across Africa's Sahel region, just south of the Sahara Desert. The 'collared' part refers to the distinctive dark marking around the back of its neck, like a partial collar or necklace that many dove species in this group display.
description: The African Collared-Dove is a small, elegant dove about 10 inches long - roughly the size of a mourning dove. Its soft plumage is pale greyish-brown on the back and wings, while the head, neck, and breast are a lovely pinkish color that fades to white on the chin and belly. Originally from Africa's arid regions, this species is extremely rare in New England, with only three recorded sightings. These birds are likely escaped or released pets, as the African Collared-Dove is the wild ancestor of the popular Barbary dove kept in captivity.

idTips.label: Pinkish Head and Breast
idTips.description: The head, neck, and upper breast show a distinctive soft pinkish wash that gradually fades to white on the chin and belly, quite different from the uniform gray-brown of most other doves

idTips.label: Pale Gray-Brown Back
idTips.description: The upper body from shoulders to tail appears pale greyish-brown with a smooth, soft texture, lighter than most common doves you'd see in New England

idTips.label: Dark Flight Feathers
idTips.description: When the wings are spread in flight, look for notably dark, almost black flight feathers that contrast sharply with the pale body

idTips.label: Bluish Wing Edge
idTips.description: The outer edge of the folded wing shows a subtle bluish tinge that catches the light, visible when the bird is perched

idTips.label: Medium Dove Size
idTips.description: About 10 inches long and stockier than a mourning dove, with the typical plump, soft-bodied build of pigeons and doves

habitat: Given their extreme rarity in New England, African Collared-Doves would most likely be spotted in urban or suburban areas, particularly around bird feeders, parks, or residential neighborhoods where escaped pet birds might survive temporarily. In their native habitat, they prefer areas near water sources in arid lands, so any New England sightings might occur near bird baths, fountains, or other reliable water sources.

seasonality.spring: Any sighting would be noteworthy year-round, but spring might offer the best chance as escaped birds attempt to establish territories and find mates.
seasonality.summer: Warm weather provides the best survival conditions for these birds adapted to arid climates, making summer sightings most plausible.
seasonality.fall: Unlikely to survive New England's cooling temperatures without supplemental feeding from humans or continued access to heated shelters.
seasonality.winter: Extremely unlikely to survive harsh New England winters outdoors, as these birds are adapted to warm, dry climates.

funFact: This dove is actually the wild ancestor of the popular pet Barbary dove - it's like seeing the 'wolf' version of a domestic dog, except in the bird world!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its close relative, the Eurasian Collared-Dove, which is much more common in North America. The African species has a distinctly pinkish head and breast, while the Eurasian Collared-Dove is more uniformly gray-brown. Remember: 'African = pinkish, Eurasian = grayish.'
contextualKnowledge: The African Collared-Dove you might spot in New England is almost certainly an escaped or released pet bird, not a wild vagrant. Pet stores often sell Barbary doves (the domestic version) and sometimes import African Collared-Doves for breeding programs, so any sighting represents a captive bird that has gained its freedom.
compareHints: Compared to its much more common relative, the Eurasian Collared-Dove, the African species is smaller and shows that distinctive pinkish wash on the head and breast instead of uniform gray-brown coloring. Both species can have dark collar markings, but the African's overall warmer, more colorful plumage sets it apart from the cooler gray tones of the Eurasian species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related African Collared-Dove is virtually identical but slightly smaller and pinker-toned – however, it's extremely rare in the wild in North America.
